extracted.intended_audience: AP English Literature teachers, exam readers, and students preparing for the AP exam
extracted.subtask_description: Scoring rubrics for AP® English Literature free-response questions 1–3 (poetry analysis, prose-fiction analysis, and literary argument), describing point-by-point criteria for Thesis, Evidence & Commentary, and Sophistication. Intended to guide scorers and inform students/teachers about what earns each point.

rubrics_metrics.name: Thesis (Question 1: Poetry Analysis) (Row A, 0-1 points)
rubrics_metrics.description: Responds to the prompt with a thesis that presents a defensible interpretation of the poem.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Scoring criteria and zero-point conditions: 0 points if there is no defensible thesis; the intended thesis only restates the prompt; the intended thesis provides a summary of the issue with no apparent or coherent claim; or there is a thesis but it does not respond to the prompt. Decision rules and scoring notes: Responses that do not earn this point only restate the prompt, make a generalized comment about the poem that doesn’t respond to the prompt, or describe the poem or features of the poem rather than making a claim that requires a defense. Responses that earn this point provide a defensible interpretation in response to the prompt. Additional notes: The thesis may be more than one sentence (provided sentences are in close proximity) and may be anywhere within the response. For a thesis to be defensible, the poem must include at least minimal evidence that could be used to support that thesis; however, the student need not cite that evidence to earn the thesis point. The thesis may establish a line of reasoning that structures the essay, but it needn’t do so to earn the thesis point. A thesis that meets the criteria can be awarded the point whether or not the rest of the response successfully supports that line of reasoning.

rubrics_metrics.name: Evidence and Commentary (Question 1: Poetry Analysis) (Row B, 0-4 points)
rubrics_metrics.description: Evaluates the quality of evidence and the explanation linking evidence to claims; scored 0–4 based on specificity of evidence and consistency/depth of commentary explaining how literary elements/techniques contribute to meaning.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Scoring grid (0–4): 0 = simply restates thesis (if present), repeats provided information, or offers information irrelevant to the prompt. 1 = EVIDENCE: provides evidence that is mostly general; COMMENTARY: summarizes the evidence but does not explain how the evidence supports the student’s argument. 2 = EVIDENCE: provides some specific, relevant evidence; COMMENTARY: explains how some of the evidence relates to the student’s argument, but no line of reasoning is established, or the line of reasoning is faulty. 3 = EVIDENCE: provides specific evidence to support all claims in a line of reasoning; COMMENTARY: explains how some of the evidence supports a line of reasoning. 4 = EVIDENCE: provides specific evidence to support all claims in a line of reasoning; COMMENTARY: consistently explains how the evidence supports a line of reasoning. Typical response descriptors: 0-point responses are incoherent or do not address the prompt, may be opinion with no textual references or irrelevant references. 1-point responses tend to focus on summary/description rather than specific details or techniques and may mention literary elements with little/no explanation. 2-point responses mix specific evidence and broad generalities, may contain simplistic/inaccurate/repetitive explanations, may make one point well but fail to support multiple claims, and do not establish clear connections. 3-point responses uniformly offer evidence to support claims. 4-point responses focus on importance of specific words/details to build interpretation; organize an argument as a line of reasoning composed of multiple supporting claims; explain how multiple literary techniques contribute to interpretation. Decision rules and additional notes: Writing that suffers from grammatical/mechanical errors that interfere with communication cannot earn the fourth point in this row. To earn the fourth point, the response may observe multiple instances of the same literary element or technique if each instance further contributes to meaning.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sophistication (Question 1: Poetry Analysis) (Row C, 0-1 points)
rubrics_metrics.description: Demonstrates sophistication of thought and/or develops a complex literary argument.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Scoring criteria: 1 point awarded for demonstration of sophistication of thought and/or development of a complex literary argument; 0 points if criteria not met. Responses that do not earn this point: attempts to contextualize that consist predominantly of sweeping generalizations; only hint at or suggest other possible interpretations; make a single statement about how an interpretation comments on something thematic without consistently maintaining that interpretation; oversimplify complexities; use complicated language ineffectively. Responses that may earn this point include any of the following: identifying and exploring complexities or tensions within the poem; illuminating the interpretation by situating it within a broader context; accounting for alternative interpretations of the poem; employing a style that is consistently vivid and persuasive. Additional note: This point should be awarded only if the sophistication or complex understanding is part of the student’s argument, not merely a phrase or reference.

rubrics_metrics.name: Thesis (Question 2: Prose Fiction Analysis) (Row A, 0-1 points)
rubrics_metrics.description: Responds to the prompt with a thesis that presents a defensible interpretation of the passage.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Scoring criteria and zero-point conditions: 0 points if there is no defensible thesis; the intended thesis only restates the prompt; the intended thesis provides a summary of the issue with no apparent or coherent claim; or there is a thesis but it does not respond to the prompt. Decision rules and scoring notes: Responses that do not earn this point only restate the prompt, make a generalized comment about the passage that doesn’t respond to the prompt, or describe the passage/features rather than make a claim requiring defense. Responses that earn this point provide a defensible interpretation in response to the prompt. Additional notes: The thesis may be more than one sentence (provided sentences are in close proximity) and may be located anywhere within the response. For a thesis to be defensible, the passage must include at least minimal evidence that could be used to support that thesis; however, the student need not cite that evidence to earn the thesis point. The thesis may establish a line of reasoning but needn’t to earn the point. A qualifying thesis can be awarded the point whether or not the rest of the response successfully supports it.

rubrics_metrics.name: Evidence and Commentary (Question 2: Prose Fiction Analysis) (Row B, 0-4 points)
rubrics_metrics.description: Assesses specific/relevant evidence from the passage and the degree to which commentary explains how literary elements/techniques contribute to meaning; scored 0–4.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Scoring grid (0–4) mirrors the poetry analysis rubric with passage-specific language: 0 = restates thesis/repeats provided info/irrelevant. 1 = evidence mostly general; commentary summarizes without explaining link to argument. 2 = some specific, relevant evidence; commentary explains some evidence-to-argument relations but lacks clear line of reasoning or is faulty. 3 = specific evidence supports claims in a line of reasoning; commentary explains how some evidence supports that line. 4 = specific evidence supports all claims; commentary consistently explains how evidence supports the line of reasoning. Typical responses: 0-point responses are incoherent or off-prompt; 1-point responses focus on overarching narrative developments or description rather than specific details/techniques; 2-point responses mix specific evidence and generalities and may not establish progression between claims; 3-point responses uniformly offer evidence to support claims; 4-point responses focus on importance of specific words/details, organize argument as a line of reasoning with multiple supporting claims each with adequate evidence clearly explained, and explain how the writer’s use of multiple literary techniques contributes to interpretation. Decision rules and additional notes: Writing with grammatical/mechanical errors that interfere with communication cannot earn the fourth point. To earn the fourth point, multiple instances of the same element may be used if each instance furthers meaning.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sophistication (Question 2: Prose Fiction Analysis) (Row C, 0-1 points)
rubrics_metrics.description: Demonstrates sophistication of thought and/or develops a complex literary argument about the passage.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Scoring criteria: 1 point for demonstrating sophistication or developing a complex literary argument; 0 points otherwise. Responses that do not earn the point: attempts at contextualization that are sweeping generalizations; only hinting at other interpretations; making a single unsupported thematic statement; oversimplifying complexities; using complex language ineffectively. Responses that may earn the point include identifying/exploring complexities or tensions within the passage; illuminating interpretation by situating it in a broader context; accounting for alternative interpretations; employing consistently vivid and persuasive style. Additional note: Award only when sophistication is integral to the argument, not merely a phrase or reference.

rubrics_metrics.name: Thesis (Question 3: Literary Argument) (Row A, 0-1 points)
rubrics_metrics.description: Responds to the prompt with a thesis that presents a defensible interpretation of the selected work.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Scoring criteria and zero-point conditions: 0 points if there is no defensible thesis; the intended thesis only restates the prompt; the intended thesis provides a summary of the issue with no apparent or coherent thesis; or there is a thesis but it does not respond to the prompt. Decision rules and scoring notes: Responses that do not earn this point only restate the prompt or make a generalized comment about the selected work that doesn’t respond to the prompt. Responses that earn this point provide a defensible interpretation in response to the prompt. Additional notes: The thesis may be multi-sentence (in close proximity) and may appear anywhere. For a thesis to be defensible, the selected work must include at least minimal evidence that could support that thesis; the student need not cite that evidence to earn the point. The thesis may establish a line of reasoning but needn’t to earn the point. A thesis meeting criteria can be awarded the point regardless of the rest of the response’s success in support.

rubrics_metrics.name: Evidence and Commentary (Question 3: Literary Argument) (Row B, 0-4 points)
rubrics_metrics.description: Judges the extent and specificity of evidence from the selected work and the quality of commentary linking evidence to claims about the work; scored 0–4.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Scoring grid (0–4) parallels earlier rubrics but with selected-work focus: 0 = restates thesis/repeats provided info/irrelevant; 1 = evidence mostly general and focuses on overarching narrative developments/description rather than specific details; 2 = some specific, relevant evidence but mixed with generalities; commentary may be simplistic or repetitive and fail to establish a line of reasoning; 3 = uniformly offer evidence to support claims; 4 = uniformly offer specific evidence, focus on important details to build interpretation, organize argument as a line of reasoning with multiple supporting claims each with adequate evidence clearly explained. Decision rules and typical-response notes: 0-point responses are incoherent or off-prompt; 1-point responses focus on broad description rather than specifics; 2-point responses may make one point well but fail to support multiple claims or show progression between claims; 3- and 4-point responses progressively demonstrate stronger evidence-integration and explanation. Additional notes: Writing that suffers from grammatical/mechanical errors that interfere with communication cannot earn the fourth point in this row. To earn the fourth point, the response must address the interpretation of the selected work as a whole.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sophistication (Question 3: Literary Argument) (Row C, 0-1 points)
rubrics_metrics.description: Demonstrates sophistication of thought and/or develops a complex literary argument about the selected work.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Scoring criteria: 1 point for demonstrating sophistication of thought and/or developing a complex literary argument; 0 points otherwise. Responses that do not earn this point: attempts to contextualize that are sweeping generalizations; only hint at other interpretations; oversimplify complexities of the topic/selected work; use complex language ineffectively. Responses that may earn the point include identifying/exploring complexities or tensions within the selected work; illuminating interpretation by situating it within a broader context; accounting for alternative interpretations; employing a consistently vivid and persuasive style. Additional note: This point should be awarded only if sophistication or complex understanding is part of the student’s argument, not merely a phrase or reference.
